ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Sampled participants were 18 years old or older, were required to be actively looking for a job, had a confirmed email address, and had agreed to receive emails and surveys.
The survey sections and item order were randomized.
Participants provided informed consent at the beginning of the survey, which adhered to the guidelines outlined in the Helsinki Protocol for Human Research and ethical standards.
Participants were asked to indicate their level of confidence for each listed behavior or outcome on a scale ranging from 0 (not at all confident) to 5 (very confident).
Participants completed Rosenberg's General Self-Esteem Scale (1965), which was translated into French by Vallieres and Vallerand (1990).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Sampled participants were 18 years old or older, were required to be actively looking for a job, had a confirmed email address, and had agreed to receive emails and surveys.

> The survey sections and item order were randomized.

> Participants provided informed consent at the beginning of the survey, which adhered to the guidelines outlined in the Helsinki Protocol for Human Research and ethical standards.

> Participants were not paid.

> Participants were asked to indicate their level of confidence for each listed behavior or outcome on a scale ranging from 0 (not at all confident) to 5 (very confident).

> Participants completed Rosenberg's General Self-Esteem Scale (1965), which was translated into French by Vallieres and Vallerand (1990).

> As preregistered, 11 participants were removed because their responses showed a variance below 0.50 across all items, and 160 respondents were removed because their responses showed a 3 Members of all categories were unemployed and required to engage in job search behavior.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Study 1 - French translation and validation of the Job Search Self-Efficacy Scale (Saks et al., 2015)
table.research_questions:
Confirmatory hypothesis (directional):
•	The scale should be a two correlated factors solution, as in the original study (structure or factor validation).
•	According to the work of Camus et al. (2017), (job-search) self-efficacy should correlate positively with the self-determined motivation subscale and negatively with the amotivation subscale of the motivation to (re)work scale
•	Job-search self-efficacy should positively correlate with Rosenberg's general self-esteem scale (1965)
•	Job-search self-efficacy should predict actual job search behaviors, as well as the outcomes of that job search (Kanfer et al., 2001; Saks et al., 2015). More precisely, following Saks et al. (2015), we posit that JSSE-B will predict jobseekers’ behavior. We also expect JSSE-O to predict jobseekers’ behavior. JSSE-B should show a larger effect than JSSE-O. JSSE-O should predict the outcomes of jobseekers’ behavior (predictive validity)
•	The scale will be administered twice to assess its stability over time. Results at T0 and T1 should be correlated (Temporal stability or test-re test reliability)

Exploratory hypothesis (non directional)
•	Job-search self-efficacy might differ in regard to socio-demographic variables;
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.q5: There is no experimental manipulation. The person who analyzes the data (first author) knows the hypothesis.
table.study_design_overview:
This study is a repeated measures observational study (or longitudinal study, panel study…). We will ask jobseekers to fill in our questionnaire twice, by email. 
We will pair jobseekers’ responses to the information system’s data of Pôle Emploi thanks to an individual identifier. We will assure jobseekers’ anonymity by using an anonymizing table preventing any link from a jobseeker’s response to his or her personal identity, except for the person who extracts and links the data (third author). The person who analyzes the data will only have access to questionnaire’s answers linked to outcomes and covariates, without any personal identifier or data.
table.randomization:
No experimental randomization of the participants into a treatment arm. 
Questionnaire sections’ order will be randomized. Items will also be randomized in each section.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.existing_data_explanation: This registration is made prior to the creation of data (questionnaires’ answers). The outcomes and covariates data exist in the information system but has neither been extracted nor observed or analyzed by any of the authors.
table.sample_size_rationale:
We draw such a large sample because:
1.	We are interested in mapping job-search self-efficacy in respect to jobseekers’ heterogeneity (age, gender…); 
2.	Data from this study will be re-used in another one, to test the hypothesis of a mediated effect of stigma consciousness on job-search behaviors through self-efficacy. More information can be found at our OSF’s research project

No formal power analysis was conducted, this large sample was determined because it should enable us to precisely map jobseekers with respect to different heterogeneity criteria.
table.stopping_rule: Data will be extracted a month after the last email wave (at the end of July 2023) to ensure a reasonable response time.
table.transformations: We will reduce and scale our data with R’s scale function when appropriate.
table.inference_criteria:
1) To assess structure or factor validity
Chi-squared’s p value should be over 0.05. We do not rely a lot on this criteria, since it is sensitive to sample size and as “N increases, its power to detect even trivial differences (…) approaches 1.0” (West et al., 2012, p. 211). Building on Hu and Bentler (1999), our 3 criteria are the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), Comparative Fit Index (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI):
•	RMSEA should be < .06 to indicate a good fit. Any value over .06 will lead to explore the reasons of this bad fit;
•	CFI should be > .95. Any value under .95 will lead to explore the reasons of this bad fit;
•	TLI should be > .95. Any value under .95 will lead to explore the reasons of this bad fit;
Exploring the reasons of a bad fit may lead us to modify our model for instance by withdrawing an item or specifying a covariance in between items. We will report all analysis and modifications departing from our plan and compare the models with the anova function when appropriate.
Cronbach’s alpha should be similar to the previous studies in which α = .89 for JSSE-B and α = .96 for JSSE-O (Saks et al., 2015).

2) To assess convergent and divergent validity
Self-esteem and self-efficacy are two very intricated concepts to such an extent that some authors include self-efficacy in their measurement of self-esteem (Harper, 1985 ; Coopersmith, 1984 ; Oubrayrie, 2005). Other authors consider self-efficacy as a distinct but linked concept to self-esteem (Martinot, 2016; Rosenberg, 1965). In this perspective, we expect the scores to Rosenberg's general self-esteem scale (1965) to positively correlate with JSSE-B and JSSE-O. We will use the traditional alpha threshold of α = 0.05 (Lakens et al., 2018).
As Camus et al. (2017) did not use this precise scale to assess the link between motivation and self-efficacy, we do not expect exact similar correlations between job-search self-efficacy and autonomous motivation or amotivation subscale. However, as job-search self-efficacy is more specific than general self-efficacy, we expect larger effects than their previous ones: r=.35 with autonomous motivation and r=-.21 with amotivation.

3) To assess predictive validity
We expect to reproduce the results of Saks et al. (2015) indicating
-	A significant link between JSSE-B and job search behavior persisting over time(β = .53; p = .00 in a first time and β = .32, p = .01 eight months later);
-	A significant link between JSSE-O and the number of job offers persisting over time (β=.27; p=.00 in a first time and β=.34; p=.01 eight months/weeks later).

4) To assess temporal stability or test-re test validity
Previous research did not assess temporal stability of the scale.
We will use the traditional alpha threshold of α = 0.05 (Lakens et al., 2018).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will exclude participants who responded in a monotonic manner to questionnaire by excluding participants whose variance lies between 0 and 0.5.
No awareness checks are included.
table.missing_data_handling: Participants who did not complete the questionnaire until the end will be removed.
table.exploratory_analyses: Job-search self-efficacy might differ according to socio-demographic variables.
table.additional_comments:
The data from this study will be reused in another study included in the same OSF project.

•	RMSEA should be < .06 to indicate a good fit. Any value over .06 will lead to explore the reasons of this bad fit;
•	CFI should be > .95. Any value under .95 will lead to explore the reasons of this bad fit;
•	TLI should be > .95. Any value under .95 will lead to explore the reasons of this bad fit;
Exploring the reasons of a bad fit may lead us to modify our model for instance by withdrawing an item or specifying a covariance in between items. We will report all analysis and modifications departing from our plan and compare the models with the anova function when appropriate.
Cronbach’s alpha should be similar to the previous studies in which α = .89 for JSSE-B and α = .96 for JSSE-O (Saks et al., 2015).

2) To assess convergent and divergent validity
Self-esteem and self-efficacy are two very intricated concepts to such an extent that some authors include self-efficacy in their measurement of self-esteem (Harper, 1985 ; Coopersmith, 1984 ; Oubrayrie, 2005). Other authors consider self-efficacy as a distinct but linked concept to self-esteem (Martinot, 2016; Rosenberg, 1965). In this perspective, we expect the scores to Rosenberg's general self-esteem scale (1965) to positively correlate with JSSE-B and JSSE-O. We will use the traditional alpha threshold of α = 0.05 (Lakens et al., 2018).
As Camus et al. (2017) did not use this precise scale to assess the link between motivation and self-efficacy, we do not expect exact similar correlations between job-search self-efficacy and autonomous motivation or amotivation subscale. However, as job-search self-efficacy is more specific than general self-efficacy, we expect larger effects than their previous ones: r=.35 with autonomous motivation and r=-.21 with amotivation.

3) To assess predictive validity
We expect to reproduce the results of Saks et al. (2015) indicating
-	A significant link between JSSE-B and job search behavior persisting over time(β = .53; p = .00 in a first time and β = .32, p = .01 eight months later);
-	A significant link between JSSE-O and the number of job offers persisting over time (β=.27; p=.00 in a first time and β=.34; p=.01 eight months/weeks later).

4) To assess temporal stability or test-re test validity
Previous research did not assess temporal stability of the scale.
We will use the traditional alpha threshold of α = 0.05 (Lakens et al., 2018).

Confirmatory outcomes are:

Our rationale is that the confirmatory outcomes depend, at least in part, on the jobseeker's behavior. Our exploratory results depend, at least in part, on external behaviors (behaviors of counselors or recruiters) and may reflect socially (de)valued self-presentation and/or self-fulfilling prophecies.

2) Covariables
Socio-demographic and covariates will be measured via Pôle emploi’s information system, to reduce questionnaire’s length:
· Age;
· Gender (Male/Female);
· Level of education, following the French training nomenclature (Lower than French Baccalauréat (Equivalent to British A-Level), without any diploma (level 6) / Lower than French Baccalauréat, with some diploma (level 5) / Lower than French Baccalauréat, with some (other) diploma (level 5 bis) / French Baccalauréat and similar (level 4) / Up to 2 years of post-secondary education (level 3) / 3 years of post-secondary education and above (level 2 and 1));
· Circumstances in which last job ended (Layoff / Contract breach / Resignation / End of fixed-term contract);
· Area of residence (QPV / Not QPV. \"QPV\" stand for Quartier prioritaires de la Politique de la Ville which might be translated as “Prioritized neighborhoods of the City Policy”. It refers to a French government urban policy scheme targeting the poorest urban areas which require more intense government intervention);
· Administrative category of the jobseeker (A / B / C);
· Length of registration at Pôle emploi in days;
· Total number of registrations at Pôle Emploi;
· Number of unemployment benefits days remaining;
· Number of meetings with the jobseeker’s counselor in the last 3 months;
· Number of rejections the person has had following an application, in the last 3 months;
· Type of Pôle Emploi’s support (Follow-up / Guided / Reinforced / Global. Pôle emploi accompanies jobseekers according to four different modalities. Suivi or follow-up is targeted as the most autonomous ones, closest to the labour market. Guidé or guided is targeted at those who need regular support in their search. Renforcé or reinforced is targeted at those who are the furthest from employment and need regular physical meetings with their counselor. Global goes even further, by setting up a pair of advisors from Pôle emploi and local councils or “conseils départementaux” to coordinate social and professionals actions);
· Number of different target jobs declared;
· Years spent working in the sector of interest;
· The job seeker is looking for a full-time job (Yes / No):
· The job seeker declared having a non-advanced level of French (Yes / No);
· Wants to become an entrepreneur (Yes / No);

Other covariates will be extracted. At the time of writing, we do not know the categories of these covariates:
· Type of employment area;
· Familial situation of the jobseeker;
· Level of qualification of the individual for the targeted job;
· Target job sector;
· Target type of contract;

3) Predictors and scales
Scales’ order is randomized. Order of the items within each scale is also randomized.

a. Job-Search Self-Efficacy (Saks et al., 2015). We translated in French the scale validated by Saks et al. (2015) following the translate/back-translate method suggested by Chapman & Carter (1979) and more recently completed by Cha et al. (2007) resulting in 21 statement after adding a supplementary one that felt missing by the consulted insertion counselor.
The scale ranges from 0 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), with a midpoint at 3 (neither agree nor disagree).

b. Rosenberg's general self-esteem scale (1965). Which has been translated in French by Vallieres & Vallerand (1990) consisting of 10 items.
Scale ranges from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 4 (Strongly agree) with 2 (Disagree) and 3 (Agree).

c. Camus et al. (2017) Motivation to (re)work scale. This scale builds on Self-Determination Theory to better understand unemployed people’s motivation in seeking a new job. More precisely, the scale consists of 5 subscales assessing autonomous motivation, motivation by identified regulation, motivation by external social and material regulation and amotivation. We present the entire scale to our participants in ordrer to preserve its internal coherence but will only be interested in the autonomous motivation and amotivation subscales as only these two should be related to job-search self-efficacy. The scale consistes in 17 items.
Scale ranges from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree).

We will calculate a mean-score for each scale or subscale.", "Analyses are made with R (R Core Team, 2021) and RStudio (RStudio Team, 2021).

We will test its structure using the package Lavaan (Rosseel, 2012). •\tA first exploratory factor analysis will be conducted with a sample of 210 randomly selected respondents (following the convention of 10 people per item);

3) To assess convergent validity, we will rely on Pearson correlations to examine the existence of a positive correlation with Rosenberg's general self-esteem scale (1965), a positive correlation with the autonomous motivation subscale of the Motivation to (re)work scale (Camus et al., 2017), a negative correlation with the amotivation subscale of the Motivation to (re)work scale (Camus et al., 2017).

4) Job-Search Self-Efficacy should predict actual job search behaviors as well as the number of received job offers (Saks et al., 2015).

Chi-squared’s p value should be over 0.05. We do not rely a lot on this criteria, since it is sensitive to sample size and as “N increases, its power to detect even trivial differences (…) approaches 1.0” (West et al., 2012, p. 211). Building on Hu and Bentler (1999), our 3 criteria are the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), Comparative Fit Index (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI):
•\tRMSEA should be < .06 to indicate a good fit. Any value over .06 will lead to explore the reasons of this bad fit;
•\tCFI should be > .95. Any value under .95 will lead to explore the reasons of this bad fit;
•\tTLI should be > .95. Any value under .95 will lead to explore the reasons of this bad fit;
Exploring the reasons of a bad fit may lead us to modify our model for instance by withdrawing an item or specifying a covariance in between items. We will report all analysis and modifications departing from our plan and compare the models with the anova function when appropriate.
Cronbach’s alpha should be similar to the previous studies in which α = .89 for JSSE-B and α = .96 for JSSE-O (Saks et al., 2015).

2) To assess convergent and divergent validity
Self-esteem and self-efficacy are two very intricated concepts to such an extent that some authors include self-efficacy in their measurement of self-esteem (Harper, 1985 ; Coopersmith, 1984 ; Oubrayrie, 2005). Other authors consider self-efficacy as a distinct but linked concept to self-esteem (Martinot, 2016; Rosenberg, 1965). In this perspective, we expect the scores to Rosenberg's general self-esteem scale (1965) to positively correlate with JSSE-B and JSSE-O. We will use the traditional alpha threshold of α = 0.05 (Lakens et al., 2018).
As Camus et al. (2017) did not use this precise scale to assess the link between motivation and self-efficacy, we do not expect exact similar correlations between job-search self-efficacy and autonomous motivation or amotivation subscale. However, as job-search self-efficacy is more specific than general self-efficacy, we expect larger effects than their previous ones: r=.35 with autonomous motivation and r=-.21 with amotivation.

3) To assess predictive validity
We expect to reproduce the results of Saks et al. (2015) indicating
-\tA significant link between JSSE-B and job search behavior persisting over time(β = .53; p = .00 in a first time and β = .32, p = .01 eight months later);
-\tA significant link between JSSE-O and the number of job offers persisting over time (β=.27; p=.00 in a first time and β=.34; p=.01 eight months/weeks later).

4) To assess temporal stability or test-re test validity
Previous research did not assess temporal stability of the scale.

We examined 173 columns across 5 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Sampled participants were 18 years old or older, were required to be actively looking for a job, had a confirmed email address, and had agreed to receive emails and surveys.
The survey sections and item order were randomized.
Participants provided informed consent at the beginning of the survey, which adhered to the guidelines outlined in the Helsinki Protocol for Human Research and ethical standards.
Participants were asked to indicate their level of confidence for each listed behavior or outcome on a scale ranging from 0 (not at all confident) to 5 (very confident).
Participants completed Rosenberg's General Self-Esteem Scale (1965), which was translated into French by Vallieres and Vallerand (1990).

As preregistered, 11 participants were removed because their responses showed a variance below 0.50 across all items, and 160 respondents were removed because their responses showed a 3 Members of all categories were unemployed and required to engage in job search behavior.

Unemployment has widespread detrimental personal, interpersonal, sociological, and economic consequences (Brand, 2015; Wanberg, 2012).
text.formatted: Unemployment has widespread detrimental personal, interpersonal, sociological, and economic consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Brand, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Wanberg, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Among its many effects, unemployment negatively affects one's physical (McKee-Ryan et al., 2005) and mental (McKee-Ryan et al., 2005; Paul & Moser, 2009), life satisfaction (Gedikli et al., 2023), selfesteem and self-efficacy (Creed et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Among its many effects, unemployment negatively affects one's physical <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(McKee-Ryan et al., 2005)</ref> and mental <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(McKee-Ryan et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Paul & Moser, 2009)</ref>, life satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gedikli et al., 2023)</ref>, selfesteem and self-efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Creed et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, individuals who become reemployed return to their baseline levels of subjective well-being, even when the working conditions are less favorable than those of their previous position (Zhou et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Conversely, individuals who become reemployed return to their baseline levels of subjective well-being, even when the working conditions are less favorable than those of their previous position <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Zhou et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, much research has been conducted on the determinants of job search behavior and subsequent employment access for unemployed people.

Among these frameworks, self-regulatory frameworks define job search as "a goaldirected, self-regulatory process in which cognition, affect, and behavior are devoted to preparing for, identifying, and pursuing job opportunities" (van Hooft et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Among these frameworks, self-regulatory frameworks define job search as "a goaldirected, self-regulatory process in which cognition, affect, and behavior are devoted to preparing for, identifying, and pursuing job opportunities" <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(van Hooft et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This job search process unfolds over time in contexts that are highly ambiguous, uncertain, and competitive (Kanfer et al., 2001; van Hooft et al., 2021; Wanberg, 2012).
text.formatted: This job search process unfolds over time in contexts that are highly ambiguous, uncertain, and competitive <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Kanfer et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">van Hooft et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Wanberg, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, individuals need to set goals, break them down into manageable plans, and initiate and sustain job search behavior in the face of multiple setbacks and degraded psychological abilities.

From this perspective, job search self-efficacy (JSSE), "the belief that one can successfully perform specific job search behaviors and obtain employment" (Saks et al., 2015, p. 115), is a central determinant of the job search process.
text.formatted: From this perspective, job search self-efficacy (JSSE), "the belief that one can successfully perform specific job search behaviors and obtain employment" <ref type="bibr">(Saks et al., 2015, p. 115)</ref>, is a central determinant of the job search process.

text.text: Theoretically, JSSE is a core component of dominant frameworks explaining the job search process.
It is related to perceived behavioral control in the theory of planned job search behavior (Ajzen, 1991; van Hooft, 2018).
text.formatted: It is related to perceived behavioral control in the theory of planned job search behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ajzen, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">van Hooft, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: It is also a key motivational resource in selfregulatory job search models, as it operates at all stages of the job search process, relating to job search goal settings, self-regulation, the intensity and quality of job search behavior, and employment outcomes, including status and quality (van Hooft et al., 2021).
text.formatted: It is also a key motivational resource in selfregulatory job search models, as it operates at all stages of the job search process, relating to job search goal settings, self-regulation, the intensity and quality of job search behavior, and employment outcomes, including status and quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(van Hooft et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Another major theoretical framework integrating job search self-efficacy is the Social Cognitive Career Theory (Lent et al., 1994), which considers JSSE as an important "proximal antecedent" of search goals, search actions and outcomes (Lent & Brown, 2013, p. 565).
text.formatted: Another major theoretical framework integrating job search self-efficacy is the Social Cognitive Career Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lent et al., 1994)</ref>, which considers JSSE as an important "proximal antecedent" of search goals, search actions and outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Lent & Brown, 2013, p. 565)</ref>.

text.text: In this specific theoretical framework, a recent meta-analysis and a recent scoping review insisted on the value of further studying JSSE and its consequences in longitudinal settings to target field interventions accordingly (Kim et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In this specific theoretical framework, a recent meta-analysis and a recent scoping review insisted on the value of further studying JSSE and its consequences in longitudinal settings to target field interventions accordingly <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kim et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Zheng et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: From an applied perspective, JSSE is of interest as it is malleable and can be targeted in job search interventions (Eden & Aviram, 1993).
text.formatted: From an applied perspective, JSSE is of interest as it is malleable and can be targeted in job search interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Eden & Aviram, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the JOBS program has been shown to increase participants' JSSE, which mediated the program's effects on job search behavior, reemployment, and mental health (Price et al., 1992; Van Ryn & Vinokur, 1992; Vinokur & Schul, 1997).
text.formatted: For example, the JOBS program has been shown to increase participants' JSSE, which mediated the program's effects on job search behavior, reemployment, and mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Price et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Van Ryn & Vinokur, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Vinokur & Schul, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, meta-analytic evidence suggests that interventions that boost self-efficacy are more effective at helping unemployed people find employment than interventions that do not target self-efficacy (Liu et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Furthermore, meta-analytic evidence suggests that interventions that boost self-efficacy are more effective at helping unemployed people find employment than interventions that do not target self-efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Liu et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, JSSE could be used to identify unemployed people with the lowest self-efficacy, who may need and benefit the most from support (Roques, 2008; van Hooft et al., 2021; Vinokur et al., 1995; Wanberg et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Finally, JSSE could be used to identify unemployed people with the lowest self-efficacy, who may need and benefit the most from support <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Roques, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">van Hooft et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Vinokur et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Wanberg et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, it is crucial for researchers focusing on the job search process and for organizations implementing programs that support unemployed people to have a reliable tool to measure JSSE.
As its definition implies, JSSE encompasses two conceptually distinct beliefs, namely the belief that one can successfully perform job search behavior and the belief that one can obtain employment.
For three decades, however, the measurement of JSSE has varied considerably from study to study, with no generally accepted scale (Saks et al., 2015).
text.formatted: For three decades, however, the measurement of JSSE has varied considerably from study to study, with no generally accepted scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Saks et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Many studies have conflated these two constructs or mixed them with others by combining items referring to job search knowledge, abilities, behavior, and outcomes into a single composite score.
To address this issue, Saks et al. (2015) constructed and validated a two-dimensional measure.
text.formatted: To address this issue, <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Saks et al. (2015)</ref> constructed and validated a two-dimensional measure.

text.text: In their study, JSSE behavior predicts job search intention and behavior, and JSSE outcome predicts the number of job offers received.
Teye-Kwadjo (2021) strengthened their work by validating the scale structure using an item response theory approach.
Taken together, these findings suggest a reliable measure of JSSE.
Building on their work, the present study translates and validates a French version of the JSSE scale while addressing four limitations of prior research.

First, we draw on a large sample of unemployed people registered with the French public employment service, of which 2,055 were used, whereas prior validations relied on smaller samples or samples of students (Saks et al., 2015; Teye-Kwadjo, 2021; Zheng et al., 2025).
text.formatted: First, we draw on a large sample of unemployed people registered with the French public employment service, of which 2,055 were used, whereas prior validations relied on smaller samples or samples of students <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Saks et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Teye-Kwadjo, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Zheng et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Second, we collected objective job search behavior and access to employment from administrative records, rather than self-reported job search behavior or employment outcomes declared by participants (Saks et al., 2015; Teye-Kwadjo, 2021; Zheng et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Second, we collected objective job search behavior and access to employment from administrative records, rather than self-reported job search behavior or employment outcomes declared by participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Saks et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Teye-Kwadjo, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Zheng et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Third, we adopted a longitudinal approach, collecting these outcomes within 90-day (three month) and 150-day (five-month), overcoming the limitations of previous cross-sectional studies (Kim et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Third, we adopted a longitudinal approach, collecting these outcomes within 90-day (three month) and 150-day (five-month), overcoming the limitations of previous cross-sectional studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kim et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Zheng et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, half of the initially sampled unemployed people was randomly assigned not to receive the survey, to rule out a potential measurement effect where measuring self-efficacy altered subsequent job search behavior (Zwane et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Fourth, half of the initially sampled unemployed people was randomly assigned not to receive the survey, to rule out a potential measurement effect where measuring self-efficacy altered subsequent job search behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Zwane et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The method and hypotheses were pre-registered (see the Methods section).

Hypotheses and research questions are divided into four categories: (1) structure and reliability of the scale, (2) validity of the scale, (3) predictive validity of the scale and (4) exploratory research questions.
Concerning the structure, we expected the scale to be a two-factor structure with correlated factors of approximately r = .69, as in the original study (H1a; Saks et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Concerning the structure, we expected the scale to be a two-factor structure with correlated factors of approximately r = .69, as in the original study (H1a; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Saks et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Its internal consistency should be close to Saks et al.'s (2015) results of α = .89 for JSSE behavior and α = .96 for JSSE outcome (H1b).
text.formatted: Its internal consistency should be close to <ref type="bibr">Saks et al.'s (2015)</ref> results of α = .89 for JSSE behavior and α = .96 for JSSE outcome (H1b).

text.text: To assess scale reliability, we expected to find a positive Pearson correlation between the JSSE subscales at T1 and T2.
Since this had not been assessed in previous research, we anticipated the correlation to be above r = .60 (H2).
Convergent validity was tested against self-esteem and motivation to (re)work.
First, self-esteem is a general evaluation of one's self-worth (Rosenberg, 1965), while JSSE is an evaluation of one's abilities in a specific domain.
text.formatted: First, self-esteem is a general evaluation of one's self-worth <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Rosenberg, 1965)</ref>, while JSSE is an evaluation of one's abilities in a specific domain.

text.text: Therefore, both belong to the broader family of self-evaluation (Kanfer et al., 2001; van Hooft et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Therefore, both belong to the broader family of self-evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Kanfer et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">van Hooft et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, we expected the scale to positively correlate with Rosenberg's (1965) self-esteem scale (H3), with a correlation equivalent to that observed by Creed et al. (2001, r = .50).
text.formatted: Accordingly, we expected the scale to positively correlate with <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Rosenberg's (1965)</ref> self-esteem scale (H3), with a correlation equivalent to that observed by <ref type="bibr">Creed et al. (2001, r = .50)</ref>.

text.text: Second, according to self-determination theory, perceived competence is a basic psychological need that supports intrinsic motivation (Ryan & Deci, 2000b).
text.formatted: Second, according to self-determination theory, perceived competence is a basic psychological need that supports intrinsic motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ryan & Deci, 2000b)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, amotivation arises from not valuing an activity, not feeling competent to perform it, or not expecting it to yield desired outcomes (Ryan & Deci, 2000a).

text.text: The latter two sources map directly onto low JSSE behavior and low JSSE outcome. Camus et al. (2017) developed a French scale to measure motivation to (re)work among unemployed people.

text.text: Consistent with this rationale, they found that general self-efficacy was positively correlated with autonomous motivation (r = .35).
However, they also found that general self-efficacy was not correlated with amotivation (r = -.21).
This null result may be due to insufficient statistical power, given that their sample size was only 54.

text.text: Regarding predictive validity, we expected JSSE to predict job search behavior as well as the outcomes of that search (Kanfer et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2019; Saks et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Regarding predictive validity, we expected JSSE to predict job search behavior as well as the outcomes of that search <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Kanfer et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Kim et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Saks et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Zheng et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We had three exploratory research questions for which we did not formulate any directional hypotheses.
First, JSSE may be related to the assistance that unemployed people receive from their job counselor, who can forward job openings that match their profile.
For example, greater JSSE could motivate individuals to complete their online profiles more thoroughly and share higher-quality resumes.
Consequently, unemployed people who display higher self-efficacy may be perceived by their counselor as better suited for available positions and, therefore, be forwarded more job openings.
However, these openings still require the unemployed person to apply, reflecting a counselor-initiated opportunity that the unemployed person then acts upon (RQ1).
Second, JSSE may be related to job proposals initiated directly by recruiters.

A higher level of self-efficacy may result in a more comprehensive and detailed profile on the public employment service's online platform, giving the impression of greater employment readiness, which may attract more direct proposals from recruiters (RQ2).

Thus, access to employment can be achieved through three channels, namely applications initiated by the unemployed person (H6), openings forwarded by a counselor (RQ1), and proposals initiated by recruiters (RQ2).
Examining these channels together helps us understand the pathways through which JSSE might relate to employment.

Finally, JSSE behavior and outcome may vary according to sociodemographic factors (age, gender, level of education, nationality, family situation, number of children to care for, length of registration with the public employment service, number of unemployment benefits days remaining, administrative category in which the person is registered, type of support from the public employment service; RQ3; Kanfer et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Finally, JSSE behavior and outcome may vary according to sociodemographic factors (age, gender, level of education, nationality, family situation, number of children to care for, length of registration with the public employment service, number of unemployment benefits days remaining, administrative category in which the person is registered, type of support from the public employment service; RQ3; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Kanfer et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Kim et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The study protocol and hypotheses were preregistered, and any deviations from the preregistration are noted.

We translated the 20-item scale by Saks et al. (2015) into French using the translate/back-translate method suggested by Chapman and Carter (Chapman & Carter, 1979) and subsequently refined by Cha et al. (Cha et al., 2007).

(2015)</ref> into French using the translate/back-translate method suggested by <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Chapman and Carter (Chapman & Carter, 1979)</ref> and subsequently refined by Cha et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Cha et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: First, three researchers from the first author's lab, who were proficient in English and not involved in the research, independently translated the original scale into French.
This resulted in three French versions of the scale.
Second, another group of three researchers from the same lab, who were also not involved in the research and unfamiliar with the original scale, compared these three versions with one another.
This working group concluded that only a few minor adjustments were necessary, as the three versions were already very similar.
Specifically, they decided to replace some words with synonyms that did not change the core Minor differences were noted, such as variations in figurative language and the use of synonyms 1 .
These differences did not affect the meaning, resulting in a good fit between the original version and its French translation.
Since the scale was intended for unemployed people, it was first presented to a group of employment counselors before being sent to unemployed people.

This group was not familiar with the research or the original scale, was tasked with determining whether the scale 1 One of the participants in this step had a British background, whereas the original scale was developed in an American context.
Some differences between the back-translated version and the original were attributed to this cultural difference.
was understandable to unemployed people, and whether it targeted the most important job search practices.
The group validated the 20-item French version of the scale and advocated for the addition of a 21 st item that they felt was missing.
This item assessed sending unsolicited job applications, an important job search strategy in the French context (Rémy & Bergeat, 2017).
text.formatted: This item assessed sending unsolicited job applications, an important job search strategy in the French context <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Rémy & Bergeat, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: It was formulated as follows: "Send unsolicited applications to get a job interview.
2 " This item was theoretically grouped with the JSSE behavior subscale.
This final step resulted in 21 statements that were tested further.
The final French scale and the original English one, along with filling instructions, can be found in Appendix 1.
This study was conducted in collaboration with France's public employment service, France Travail.
It provides services to unemployed people, supports employers in their recruitment processes, and facilitates employment policies at the national and regional levels.
Its most popular service is providing unemployment benefits to eligible individuals, which encourages people to register with the organization.
A random sample of 60,000 unemployed people was extracted, from a total pool of approximately 5,000,000 registered individuals, in June 2023.
Sampled participants were 18 years old or older, were required to be actively looking for a job, had a confirmed email address, and had agreed to receive emails and surveys.
To test for a measurement effect, half of the sample was randomly assigned to receive the survey, while the other half was not.
The survey sections and item order were randomized.
Participants provided informed consent at the beginning of the survey, which adhered to the guidelines outlined in the Helsinki Protocol for Human Research and ethical standards.
Participants were not paid.
Participation was clearly stated to be voluntary and anonymous, with no possible consequences for participants or their unemployment benefits.
2 "Faire des candidatures spontanées pour obtenir un entretien d'embauche."
Unemployed people were emailed twice to complete a survey.
The first email was sent in early June 2023 (T1), and the second was sent at the end of June to ensure a one-month interval between responses (T2).
A reminder email was sent one week after each initial email.
Answers were paired with data from the public employment service's information system using an individual identifier and an anonymizing table.
This made it possible to extract job search behavior and access to employment within 90-day (three months) and 150-day (five months), respectively.

The internal consistency of each scale was assessed by computing hierarchical omega and Cronbach's alpha, along with their bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) 10,000 bootstrap confidence intervals (Kelley, 2026).
text.formatted: The internal consistency of each scale was assessed by computing hierarchical omega and Cronbach's alpha, along with their bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) 10,000 bootstrap confidence intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Kelley, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The French version of the JSSE scale consists of 21 statements, such as "Prepare a sales pitch that will attract the interest of employers" (JSSE behavior) or "Obtain more than one good job offer" (JSSE outcome).
Participants were asked to indicate their level of confidence for each listed behavior or outcome on a scale ranging from 0 (not at all confident) to 5 (very confident).
Internal consistency indices are reported in the Results section.
Participants completed Rosenberg's General Self-Esteem Scale (1965), which was translated into French by Vallieres and Vallerand (1990).
text.formatted: Participants completed Rosenberg's General Self-Esteem Scale (1965), which was translated into French by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Vallieres and Vallerand (1990)</ref>.

text.text: The scale consists of ten items, such as "On the whole, I am satisfied with myself", with which participants indicate their level of agreement on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
The scale had good internal consistency (α = .85 [.83; .86]; ω = .84 [.83; .86]).
Participants answered the Motivation to (Re)work Scale by Camus et al. (2017).
text.formatted: Participants answered the Motivation to (Re)work Scale by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Camus et al. (2017)</ref>.

text.text: The scale consists of five subscales that assess autonomous motivation, identified regulation, external social regulation, external material regulation, and amotivation.
Although the entire scale was presented to preserve its coherence, we only had hypotheses about the autonomous motivation and amotivation subscales, as only these two are related to JSSE.
The scale contains 17 items, such as "I want to go back to work because I really enjoy it" (autonomous motivation) and "I don't see the point of going back to work" (amotivation).
Participants indicated their level of agreement with each item on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

The scale had good internal consistency for the autonomous motivation (α = .85 [.84; .87]; ω = .85 [.84; .87]), the identified regulation (α = .76 [.74; .78]; ω = .76 [.74; .78]), external social regulation (α = .64 [.61; .67]; ω = .70 [.66; .73]), external material regulation (α = .74 [.71; .76]; ω = .75 [.72; .77]), and amotivation (α = .76 [.73; .79]; ω = .76 [.73; .79]) subscales.
Behavioral outcomes were extracted from the public employment service's information system 90 days (three months) after the initial survey was sent out.

For unemployed people, the behavioral measures were the number of job applications submitted, the number of clicks on job postings on the public employment service platform, and the amount of time spent on the platform.
For job counselors, the behavioral measures were the number of job openings the counselor forwarded to the unemployed person.
For recruiters, the behavioral measures were the number of proposals a recruiter sent to the unemployed person through the platform.
All behavioral outcomes were winsorized at the 99 th percentile (values above that threshold were recoded to that threshold's value).
Although it was not pre-registered, we created a job search engagement score to complement the single-behavior count outcomes.
This score deliberately combined both flow and stock indicators to provide a broader, more sensitive exploratory summary of overall job search engagement.

Six binary indicators were aggregated, and one point was assigned for each of the following: sending at least one application within 90 days; clicking on at least one job posting within 90 days; visiting the platform at least once within 90 days; having created an online profile on the public employment service website; having uploaded a résumé to the online platform; and having made this profile publicly accessible to recruiters.

Job search outcomes were drawn from objective administrative records 150-day (five months) after the initial survey was sent out, capturing whether the person obtained employment anywhere in the country.

The preregistration identified two types of employment outcomes: precarious employment, which includes temporary agency work and fixed-term contracts shorter than six months, and stable employment, which includes permanent contracts.
However, the information system did not record contract duration, so the precarious employment category could not be constructed.
Therefore, we report employment at the level of detail available in the administrative records.
This decomposition is more detailed than the preregistered dichotomy, and we consider this deviation to increase the informativeness of the employment analyses.
Contrary to our expectations, the information as to whether a person created a company was not available among the extracted data.
Therefore, we could not include this specific outcome in our analysis.

As pre-registered, to further test the hypothesis that a two-factor model best fits the scale (H1a), a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted on the remaining sample of 1,845 participants using a robust maximum likelihood estimation.

The two latent factors were strongly correlated (r = .89 [.87; .91]), exceeding the correlation reported by Saks et al. (2015; r = .69).

The item added by job counselors, related to sending unsolicited applications to get a job interview, loaded on the JSSE behavior subscale with standardized λ = .70 [.67; .73], indicating that the added item behaves consistently with the original scale.

As anticipated in our pre-registration and because the two-factor model did not fully meet the pre-specified fit criteria, we inspected the modification indices to locate the main source of local misfit.
The largest one corresponded to a residual covariance between items "Get a job as soon as possible" and "Be invited for site visits."

As both items refer to achieving concrete outcomes of the job search rather than enacting search behaviors, which plausibly produces shared variance beyond the common factor, we freely estimated this residual covariance.
Adding this parameter improved the fit, with the scale meeting the prespecified cutoffs (χ² = 793(187), p < .001, RMSEA = .052 [.049,.056], CFI = .960, TLI = .955, SRMR = .033).

text.text: We 433 tested configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance.
The configural model estimated the 434 two-factor structure freely in each group and served as the baseline.
The metric model 435 constrained factor loadings to be equal across groups.
The scalar model constrained item 436 intercepts as well.
The strict model constrained residual variances as well.

Overall, the scale demonstrated strict invariance across age, gender, level of education, 438 and length of registration, indicating that loadings, intercepts, and residual variances were 439 equivalent.
It further demonstrated scalar invariance across time, with loadings and intercepts equivalent at T1 and T2 and only minor differences in residual variances.

This finding supports the comparison of latent means, structural parameters, and observed composite scores across these groups, and interpreting the test-retest correlations as reflecting temporal stability of the construct rather than a change in its measurement.

text.text: As shown in Appendix 2, respondents differed from non-respondents on nearly all measured sociodemographics.

To check that this did not bias our results, we re-estimated all predictive models using inverse-probability weighting, which weights respondents by the inverse of their estimated probability of responding.
The predictors of responding to the survey were selected by LASSO regression.
Full results are reported in Appendix 6.
The signs and magnitudes were comparable to those of the main analyses across all outcomes and predictors.
JSSE behavior remained positively associated with the number of applications sent, the probability of sending at least one application, and job search engagement.
JSSE outcome remained negatively associated with behavioral outcomes.
The associations with access to employment were also unchanged, with JSSE behavior predicting permanent employment, and JSSE outcome predicting temporary agency work.
Since these weights correct for observed differences between respondents and non-respondents, the stability of the results suggests that observed selection does not drive our conclusions.
However, selection based on unobserved characteristics, such as non-respondents' selfesteem, cannot be ruled out as these weights only correct for the observed covariates included in the model.

This study translated and validated a French version of the job search self-efficacy (JSSE) scale developed by Saks et al. (2015) among a large sample of unemployed people, assessing its structure, reliability, convergent and predictive validity.

(2015)</ref> among a large sample of unemployed people, assessing its structure, reliability, convergent and predictive validity.

text.text: Consistent with H1a, both exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses showed that a two-factor solution reproduced the theoretical distinction between JSSE behavior and JSSE outcome, and fitted better than a one-factor solution.
These results were replicated when accounting for the ordinal nature of the items.
The correlations between the two latent factors, as well as between the two observed factors, were stronger than reported by Saks et al. (2015).
text.formatted: The correlations between the two latent factors, as well as between the two observed factors, were stronger than reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Saks et al. (2015)</ref>.

text.text: Exploratory measurement invariance testing showed that strict invariance held across age, gender, level of education and length of registration, while scalar invariance was found across a one-month interval.
The two-factor confirmatory model did not meet the more stringent dynamic fit index cutoffs (McNeish & Wolf, 2023).
text.formatted: The two-factor confirmatory model did not meet the more stringent dynamic fit index cutoffs <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(McNeish & Wolf, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with H1b, both subscales showed strong reliability, with omegas and alphas above .90, in line with Saks et al. (2015).
text.formatted: Consistent with H1b, both subscales showed strong reliability, with omegas and alphas above .90, in line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Saks et al. (2015)</ref>.

text.text: Supporting H2, the test-retest reliability of the scale over a one-month interval was excellent, with Pearson correlations above r = .72 and confidence intervals excluding .60.

Considered jointly, these results indicate a two-factor scale that is coherent with the theoretical distinction between JSSE behavior and JSSE outcome, although latent factors were strongly correlated.
Supporting H3, H4a and H4b, both subscales correlated in the expected direction with self-esteem, autonomous motivation to (re)work, and amotivation to (re)work, respectively.
Contrary to expectation, the correlations with self-esteem were not equivalent to that reported by Creed et al. (2001; r = .50), but were close.
text.formatted: Contrary to expectation, the correlations with self-esteem were not equivalent to that reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Creed et al. (2001</ref>; r = .50), but were close.

text.text: Contrary to our expectation, correlations with autonomous motivation and amotivation were not stronger than those reported by Camus et al. (2017), the former being equivalent and the latter slightly weaker.
text.formatted: Contrary to our expectation, correlations with autonomous motivation and amotivation were not stronger than those reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Camus et al. (2017)</ref>, the former being equivalent and the latter slightly weaker.

text.text: Exploratory analyses further showed that both subscales were essentially unrelated to identified regulation, very weakly and negatively related to external social motivation, and weakly and positively related to external material motivation.
These associations position JSSE along the self-determination continuum, correlating most strongly with autonomous motivation and negatively with amotivation.
This supports the idea that JSSE is a domain-specific evaluation of one's abilities rather than a general motivation proxy or a general self-evaluation.
In sum, these results place JSSE as a proximal but distinct concept from motivation and self-esteem.
Consistent with H5a, JSSE behavior positively predicted the number of applications sent, the probability of sending at least one application, and overall job search engagement.
However, it was not a predictor of platform browsing behavior, such as the time spent viewing job ads, the number of clicks on job offers, or the probability of engaging in these activities.
Nevertheless, all of these coefficients pointed in the expected positive direction, and several approached significance.
Thus, H5a was only partially supported.
Theoretically, JSSE behavior is related to action and concrete goal setting (Lent & Brown, 2013; van Hooft et al., 2021) and targets "specific job search behaviors" (Saks et al., 2015, p. 105).
text.formatted: Theoretically, JSSE behavior is related to action and concrete goal setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lent & Brown, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">van Hooft et al., 2021)</ref> and targets "specific job search behaviors" <ref type="bibr">(Saks et al., 2015, p. 105)</ref>.

text.text: Our results are consistent with this definition, as sending an application is a discrete, self-initiated act with the clear objective to obtain an interview and, ultimately, a job.
In contrast, browsing or clicking on job ads is diffuse and only serves the intermediate goal of finding opportunities.
Its payoff largely lies outside the individual's control since time spent searching may or may not yield results.

Thus, our overall pattern of results supports the idea that JSSE behavior relates to specific, targeted job search activities, such as sending applications, rather than to more general activities, such as browsing employment platforms.

This aligns with Kim et al.'s (2019, p. 28) conclusion that JSSE behaviors "have a more meaningful relationship with the activities and resources used for job searching than with the actual time spent in the job search."
text.formatted: This aligns with <ref type="bibr">Kim et al.'s (2019, p. 28)</ref> conclusion that JSSE behaviors "have a more meaningful relationship with the activities and resources used for job searching than with the actual time spent in the job search."

text.text: Contrary to H5b, JSSE outcome negatively predicted all of these behaviors.
Since the two subscales were highly correlated, including them in the same model means that each coefficient reflects only the unique variance of one subscale when the other is held constant.

This should not be interpreted as evidence that expecting favorable outcomes reduces job searching, but suggests that, among individuals with the same level of JSSE behavior, those with higher JSSE outcome search less.
H5c assumed two positive effects, with a stronger coefficient for JSSE behavior than for JSSE outcome, and is not supported on either count.
First, the two subscales predicted job search behavior in opposite rather than similar directions.
Second, the absolute effects did not differ in magnitude across all outcomes.
Contrary to H6, JSSE behavior predicted a higher likelihood of obtaining a permanent job, and a lower likelihood of obtaining a temporary agency job.
Moreover, also contrary to H6, JSSE outcome only predicted access to a temporary agency job.
Therefore, when job search effort is held constant, individuals who are more confident in their ability to obtain employment are more likely to enter temporary agency work.
In contrast, individuals who are more confident in their ability to conduct the job search itself are less likely to do so and more likely to obtain a permanent job.
One interpretation is that JSSE outcome captures confidence in obtaining any kind of employment, regardless of its quality or stability.
Under this reading, unemployed people high in JSSE outcome would be more available for readily accessible positions, of which temporary agency work is the most immediate and least selective.
JSSE behavior, on the other hand, could support a sustained and targeted job search and could therefore orient unemployed people toward permanent employment.
However, this interpretation should be taken with caution as it is post hoc.
Overall, contrary to H6, access to employment was largely unrelated to JSSE.

This finding is consistent with the idea that selfefficacy is a proximal determinant of job search behavior, but a distal predictor of employment, which depends heavily on labor market conditions and employer decisions that lie beyond the individual (Kanfer et al., 2001; Lent & Brown, 2013).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with the idea that selfefficacy is a proximal determinant of job search behavior, but a distal predictor of employment, which depends heavily on labor market conditions and employer decisions that lie beyond the individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Kanfer et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Lent & Brown, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In response to RQ1 and RQ2, neither JSSE behavior nor JSSE outcome predicted the number of job openings forwarded by a counselor, the number of job proposals initiated by a recruiter, nor the probability of receiving at least one of these.
Therefore, these two channels to employment were unrelated to JSSE, complementing the results of H6.

Considered as a whole, the convergence across the three channels reinforces the idea that self-efficacy is a proximal determinant of job search behavior for unemployed people, but a distal predictor of employment that lies beyond one's behavior, as well as the judgments and decisions of counselors and recruiters.
Finally, addressing RQ3, JSSE behavior and outcome varied according to several sociodemographic characteristics.
Since all predictors were included in the models, these are partial associations adjusted for the remaining covariates.
Specifically, men, non-French participants, and participants with dependent children reported higher self-efficacy, primarily on JSSE outcome.
In contrast, participants with no diploma reported lower JSSE behavior, and those seeking part-time open-ended contracts reported lower self-efficacy on both subscales.
We had no specific hypotheses about these associations and present them as exploratory findings.
The clearest pattern was related to the intensity of support provided by the employment service.
Unemployed people who received guided, reinforced, or very reinforced support reported progressively lower JSSE behavior and outcome than those who received regular follow-up.
The fact that the scale tracks this is a favorable sign for its validity and supports its use in identifying unemployed people who may benefit the most from targeted intervention.
These results support the validity of the French translation of the JSSE scale, at least among unemployed people in France.

This conclusion is supported by several strengths that address limitations of prior research, including a large sample size of 2,055 unemployed people, objective indicators of job search behavior and access to employment drawn from administrative records, a longitudinal design spanning 90-and 150-day windows, and the ruling out of a measurement effect (Saks et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2025).

text.text: The signs and magnitudes were comparable across all outcomes and predictors, indicating that the observed selection does not drive our conclusions.
In this study, we thoroughly translated and validated the Job Search Self-Efficacy Scale among unemployed people in France.

The French version reproduced the original's two-factor structure, demonstrated high reliability, remained stable over one month, and was largely invariant across age, gender, education level, unemployment duration, and across a one-month interval.
This makes the French version suitable for research and applied use, as well as for comparing groups of unemployed people.
Furthermore, job search self-efficacy behavior positively predicted the number of job applications sent within 90 days, while job search self-efficacy outcome negatively predicted it.

Finally, job search self-efficacy behavior positively predicted access to a permanent job and negatively predicted access to a temporary agency job, while job search self-efficacy outcome only predicted access to a temporary agency job.
However, the two subscales were very strongly correlated in this population, and their distinct predictive value should be better established.
Overall, the French JSSE scale is a psychometrically sound measure that can support future research and interventions on job searching in French-speaking settings.

text.text: By translating a validated and coherent scale into French, we provide French-speaking scholars with a measure that distinguishes JSSE behavior from JSSE outcome, which is valuable in multiple theoretical frameworks that include self-efficacy as a component of models aiming to explore the job search process.
Further validation beyond the French unemployment context is pending.

The scale could also benefit applied settings, as its temporal stability makes it suitable for evaluating the effectiveness of interventions in improving JSSE (Eden & Aviram, 1993; Liu et al., 2014; Price et al., 1992; Roques, 2008; Van Ryn & Vinokur, 1992; Vinokur & Schul, 1997).

text.text: Additionally, its ability to identify unemployed people most in need of support, as demonstrated by its correlation with the level of support provided by the employment service, is valuable for pinpointing unemployed people who require additional assistance (van Hooft et al., 2021; Wanberg et al., 2010).

text.text: Future research could define thresholds that would help both researchers and practitioners in identifying unemployed people in need of specific help with their job search.
The first limitation is that, in this sample, the two subscales were highly correlated at the observed level, and very highly at the latent level.
While remaining structurally distinct and invariant, the two subscales shared much of their variance and largely measured the same construct.
On a positive note, the regression models did not show elevated variance inflation factors.

Future studies could use cognitive interviewing to determine if respondents can distinguish between the two sets of items and examine if the subscales provide distinct predictive information in samples where the two beliefs are less correlated.
In addition to the strong covariance between the subscales, the internal consistency within each subscale is high.
The alphas and omegas for the JSSE behavior subscale reach the threshold of .90, while the alphas and omegas for the JSSE outcome subscale exceed it.
While this result aligns with that of Saks et al. (2015), it also suggests that some items are redundant.

text.text: Future research could focus on creating a shorter version of the scale to reduce redundancy and improve usability.
Second, job search behavior and access to employment were obtained from the information system of the French public employment service.
While this yields objective and unobtrusive measures, it only captures job search activity recorded on the public platform.

Although the database contains over one million job openings and is a valuable resource, participants may have used it infrequently, browsed without logging in, or relied on other job boards whose usage records we could not access.
Thus, part of their true job search effort went unobserved, which may weaken the associations with self-efficacy.

Nevertheless, we consider the administrative measure a strength because Marinescu and Skandalis (2021) have demonstrated that the database and its online applications reliably capture the overall job search process.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, we consider the administrative measure a strength because <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Marinescu and Skandalis (2021)</ref> have demonstrated that the database and its online applications reliably capture the overall job search process.

text.text: Another limitation is that our job search behavior and job search outcome measures differed from those of Saks et al. (2015), who used self-reported job search behavior and the number of job offers received.

Thus, the two approaches provide complementary evidence from different measurement perspectives.

Third, the response rate was low, and respondents differed markedly from nonrespondents on nearly all observed characteristics (Appendix 2), consistent with an overrepresentation of more engaged unemployed people.
To address this selection, robustness analyses reweighting the sample by the inverse probability of responding were conducted.

To test whether JSSE behavior (H5a) and JSSE outcome (H5b) would predict job search behavior, we regressed the number of applications sent within 90 days, whether the person sent at least one application within 90 days, the time spent looking at job ads within 90 days, whether the person spent any time looking at job ads within 90 days, the number of clicks on job offers within 90 days, whether the person clicked on at least one ad on the job search platform, and a general job search engagement, on JSSE behavior, JSSE outcome, with covariates listed above.

To test whether JSSE behavior would have a stronger effect than JSSE outcome (H5c), the average marginal effects on the response scale were compared, using "HC3" robust standard errors (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024).
Results are reported in Table5.
Number of applications sent within 90 days.

JSSE behavior was associated with a higher application count (IRR = 1.40 [1.07; 1.83], SE = 0.19, z = 2.44, p = .015), while JSSE outcome was associated with a lower count (IRR = 0.69 [0.54; 0.88], SE = 0.08, z = -3.03, p = .002).
On the response scale, this represents 0.17 [0.03; 0.31] more applications for a onepoint increase in JSSE behavior, and -0.19 [-0.31; -0.06] for a one-point increase in JSSE outcome.
The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly smaller than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.02 [-0.10; 0.07], p = .678).
Sending at least one application within 90 days.

JSSE behavior was associated with higher odds of sending at least one application (OR = 1.35 [1.05; 1.75], SE = 0.18, z = 2.32, p = .021), while JSSE outcome was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.75 [0.60; 0.94], SE = 0.08, z = -2.55, p = .011).
On the probability scale, a one-point increase in JSSE behavior raised the likelihood of sending an application by 3.58 [0.55; 6.60] percentage points.
Conversely, an increase of one point in JSSE outcome lowered the likelihood by -3.42 [6.04; -0.80] percentage points.
The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly larger than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = 0.16 [-1.61; 1.92], p = .861).
Time spent looking at job ads within 90 days.

JSSE behavior was not associated with time spent (IRR = 1.31 [0.95; 1.81], SE = 0.22, z = 1.62, p = .105), but JSSE outcome was associated with spending less time (IRR = 0.74 [0.56; 0.97], SE = 0.10, z = -2.18, p = .030).
On the response scale, a one-point increase in JSSE outcome corresponded to -1.54 [-2.97; -0.12] minutes spent on the platform.
The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly weaker than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.19 [-1.18; 0.80], p = .705).
Spending any time looking at job ads within 90 days.

JSSE behavior was not associated with spending time on job ads (OR = 1.24 [0.97; 1.59], SE = 0.15, z = 1.75, p = .081), whereas JSSE outcome was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.78 [0.63; 0.97], SE = 0.09, z = -2.19, p = .029).
On the probability scale, a one-point increase in JSSE outcome lowered the likelihood of spending time on job ads by -2.99 [-5.66; -0.31] percentage points.
The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly smaller than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.31 [-2.14; 1.51], p = .737).
Number of clicks on job offers within 90 days.
JSSE behavior was not associated with the number of clicks (IRR = 1.30 [0.99; 1.70], SE = 0.18, z = 1.88, p = .060).
However, JSSE outcome was associated with fewer clicks (IRR = 0.72 [0.57; 0.92], SE = 0.09, z = -2.69, p = .007).
On the response scale, a one-point increase in JSSE outcome corresponded to approximately -0.37 [-0.65; -0.09] clicks.
The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly weaker than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.08 [-0.27; 0.12], p = .434).
At least one click on the job search platform.
JSSE behavior was not associated with clicking on job offers (OR = 1.23 [0.98; 1.53], SE = 0.14, z = 1.77, p = .076).
JSSE outcome was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.81 [0.66; 0.99], SE = 0.08, z = -2.09, p = .037).
On the probability scale, a one-point increase in JSSE outcome lowered the likelihood of clicking on a job offer by -3.04 [-5.90; -0.19] percentage points.
The absolute effect of JSSE behavior was slightly weaker than that of JSSE outcome on the response scale, and the two did not differ in magnitude (Δ = -0.15 [-2.08; 1.77], p = .877).
Any kind of job (permanent, fixed term, or temporary agency employment).
JSSE behavior was not associated with obtaining any job (OR = 0.93 [0.76; 1.14], SE = 0.10, z = -0.67, p = .506).
Similarly, JSSE outcome was not associated with obtaining any job (OR = 1.09 [0.91; 1.30], SE = 0.10, z = 0.96, p = .338).
Any standard employment (permanent or fixed term employment).
JSSE behavior was not associated with obtaining standard employment (OR = 1.13 [0.91; 1.40], SE = 0.12, z = 1.10, p = .271).
Similarly, JSSE outcome was not associated with obtaining standard employment (OR = 0.97 [0.81; 1.17], SE = 0.09, z = -0.29, p = .769).
